opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real case on both sides, and I go back and forth on it more than people might assume.

The case for going straight-shot is fairly simple. When you're in the market, you're in a rat race. You have to compete, ship products, make difficult trade-offs on how much compute goes to research versus serving customers, and the pressure of that environment pulls you in directions that aren't necessarily the ones that matter most for getting the fundamental thing right. Being insulated from that is valuable. It lets you focus on the research, on the ideas you believe in, without needing to justify every quarter in terms of revenue.

But there's a counterargument I take seriously too. It's actually very useful for the world to see powerful AI. It's hard to communicate what this technology is going to be like. You can write essays, you can give talks, but people don't really internalize it until they experience it. And that matters for safety, because governments, companies, and the public will only behave appropriately once they feel the power of the thing. So gradual deployment has real merit: it gives society time to adjust and gives you feedback about where things break.

So where I land is something like this: the straight-shot plan is attractive, but I don't think it should be treated as dogma. It could be that timelines turn out longer than expected, or that it becomes clearly valuable to show something along the way. The deeper point is that whatever path you take, the thing you're ultimately building should be robustly aligned and should care about sentient life. That matters more than the specific go-to-market strategy.

r001.rationale: The response says market participation creates a rat race and forces difficult trade-offs between research compute and serving customers.

r002.rationale: It says essays and talks do not make people internalize what powerful AI will be like; they need to experience it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a really good question, and I'll tell you how I think about it.

The conventional path, which almost everyone is taking, is that you enter the market, you build products, you generate revenue, you use that revenue and the data and the feedback loops to fund the next generation of models, and you iterate your way up. And there's a lot of logic to it. It's not crazy. It's how most of the companies that are at the frontier today got to where they are.

But I think there is something that gets lost when you do that. When you're in the market, you're in a race. And in a race, you're constantly optimizing for the thing that ships next quarter. You're making a lot of compromises, and each compromise individually seems small, but they add up. The research agenda becomes subordinate to the product agenda. And the thing about superintelligence is that it's not a product. It's a different kind of object entirely. The questions you need to answer to get there safely, the questions about alignment, about what the system actually wants, about how you make it so that it's robustly good, those are not the questions that the market rewards you for answering. The market rewards you for the model being a bit better at coding than the other guy's model.

So the bet we're making is pretty simple. We think the actual hard problem is a research problem, and that research gets done better when it's insulated from the commercial pressure. You get to think for a few years. You get to be wrong and change your mind without a stock price reacting to it. And you get to build the thing right the first time rather than retrofitting safety onto something that was designed for a different purpose.

Now, the obvious objection is, well, how do you know you'll have enough compute? How do you keep up? And that's a real concern, I won't pretend otherwise. The way I'd put it is that the amount of compute you need to do the research is a lot less than the amount of compute you need to serve a hundred million users. Those are very different numbers. And I think a lot of people conflate them. The thing that makes the market path expensive is the serving, not the thinking.

The other thing I'd say is that I think the timelines are such that this isn't a thirty-year project. If I thought it was thirty years, then sure, you need a business to sustain yourself. But if it's the kind of thing where the key ideas can come together in a handful of years, then a focused effort with the right people and enough compute to run real experiments is a very reasonable bet. Maybe it's the only reasonable bet, actually, if you take the goal seriously.

And then the last part, and this is the part I feel most strongly about, is that someone has to be doing it this way. Even if I'm wrong about the specifics, I think it's important that there is at least one serious effort whose only job is to get this right, and that isn't distracted by anything else. Because if every frontier lab is racing on products, then the thing that matters most gets the least attention. So that's the case. It's a bet. But I think it's the right bet.

r001.rationale: It says that entering the market puts developers in a race to ship, forcing compromises and making the research agenda subordinate to product demands.

r002.rationale: The response discusses building and researching superintelligence, but does not argue that the world must be exposed to powerful AI to communicate the AI itself rather than only its idea.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is focus. If you believe you have a promising approach to building safe superintelligence, then you can organize all your effort around that. You don’t have to maintain a product or make a series of decisions about what customers need next quarter.

But there is a real tradeoff. Products give you feedback. You learn things from deployment that you might not learn in a lab. And, of course, revenue helps pay for research. So the question is whether those benefits outweigh the distraction for the particular research program you’re pursuing.

I don’t think there is an answer that applies to every company. A direct path makes sense if you have enough confidence in your research direction and enough resources to give it time. The hard part is that you’re making that decision under uncertainty. You still need evidence that you’re making progress; choosing not to enter the market doesn’t remove that requirement.

r001.rationale: The response describes market participation as a source of distraction and trade-offs, but does not identify competitive pressure as a source.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that exposing the world to powerful AI is necessary to communicate the AI itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest argument for going directly is focus. If you believe there is still important research to do, then having a product creates a second set of demands. You need to serve customers, improve reliability, compete. Those are real demands, and they can pull you toward work that is useful commercially but isn’t the research you most need to do.

The argument on the other side is also strong. A product gives you resources, and contact with reality. You learn things from deployment that you might not learn in a lab. And if the research takes longer than you expect, having a business is very valuable.

So I don’t think there is a universal answer. It depends on whether you have a research direction you believe in, and whether you can give yourself enough time to pursue it. Going directly means accepting that you won’t have the same intermediate feedback. You have to be willing to make that bet—and still be very honest with yourself about whether you’re making progress.

r001.rationale: The response says a product brings competitive demands that can pull developers toward commercially useful work and away from needed research.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning from deployment, but does not argue that exposing the world to powerful AI is necessary to communicate the AI itself rather than just the idea.
